blocks.x: You can just give your name then. My name is Rick Carter Lexus. I was born in New Orleans, Louisiana in 1896. You have the exact date? On the 16th date of October. And my mother and father moved from New Orleans and moved over to Basin Lewis, which my father was a professor of violin player, taught music. You can just sit back and relax. It'll pick up anything. And I went to school in Basin Lewis. When did you move over there? You moved either barn here, but then moved over. My father and mother moved over. I was a baby in the home and my oldest brother, Joseph Alexis, he was a little kid walking. Then after getting over there, my mother had four children. She had 14 children. Fourteen. And, uh… Were you next to the oldest? I'm next to the oldest. My oldest brother was dead. He was a great drummer. He was a star drummer with Sam Morgan's band here in New Orleans years ago. That's fair to have you. And we played, we both played with my father's band. I took a drum first. I gave up the drum on the count of my brother playing drums. My father came to New Orleans and bought a trumpet, a cornet then wasn't no trumpets, a cornet from Henry Davis, which he dropped days playing a few of them. Years after that. But it was the first trumpet that I blew was Henry Davis, a well-known trumpet player in New Orleans. And I played with my father's band on trumpet. Taught me music. What kind of a band did he have? A dance band or was it a concert style or what? It would be what you call a Dixieland band here today. It used trombone, clarinet.
So I was asking about the brass bands over...

They had one in Bay St. Louis. They came here and played for the, I think, the Nardipede Club or something. They had little brass horns, and the iron tone was a little horn, and the guys over here, they looked down like they were the craziest and all that. They thought, you know, it was so funny the way the funny-looking instruments they had. But when they cracked down, they eyes open. They had the same old brass bands and Bay St. Louis. They tore up in the audience. And those were the St. Catherine Hall of St. Peter Claver, they kept in the corner.
Chinese, is that something about Chinese?

Chinese, they were all sorts. I let them go several times on account of drinking so hard. And blowing up a job right there in Biloxi. He dropped around out of the truck, so he got Saeed, sent it back to New York.
He said he'd entice you to come in the band, Shani, huh?

Shani met me on Rampo in Tulane. He was getting the shoes shined. I got on the stand, I got a shot. They were playing at Millersburg that day. He said, Rick, take a ride out there. Another boy was playing out, and I used to do it. I cooled all out there with her.
Excuse me to interrupt, but how'd you get out there? How'd you get out to Millersburg?
For a smoke and mirror.
He told her, look, I had a shake side to side.
Shake side over the place. Well, when we get out there,

I was glad to see that. I asked her to play a few numbers for me. So I sat in the band, Tiki Long. I only had one trumpet then. And I played a few numbers, and they all liked it. And Emma kept looking at me, and she was like she fell in love with me. And I left for my dad. She called me up the next day. That started romance. We went together. I got a son with her. I'm 35 years old right now. I know.
Well, I met your son one time over in Piqu. Oh, yeah. Opened his place up on London that time, and you had your band up there. Your son was there.

So after that, it was like she fell in love with me. She was going with Baby Dots. And I took her away from Baby Dots. And she got to talk to Celestan. And Johnny got to talk to him. And Celestan took me in the band.
Baby always asked me every time I go to New Orleans, did you see Emma Barrett? How's Emma? I took her from him. Was that before you then? He knew it.

He kept me about that in New York. The last time I was up there, he was kidding me about it. He was shivering himself with an electric shield. And he said, Rick, you ought to wrap down the club. He took my gala joy. Right in his house. We was supposed to go out of him. Him and I. Him and I and Red Island. And he, uh...
Tell me, how did Baby play in the old days? Oh, he was good. Was he always good? I know he's good now. Of course, he has a stroke now. But I mean, I never heard him in the old days. All right.
Baby Dodds and Johnny Dodds, they raised in Wayland, Mississippi. They used to walk from Wayland to Basin, Lewis, to go to school. We went to school together. Oh, I didn't know.
He didn't know me.
He didn't know me. Baby Dodds, they don't know the old family. That's where they come from. They're amazing.
Yeah, I do know.

Well, they went to school in Basin, Lewis, right with us, side by side. Johnny and Baby. My father knows that father and mother are all just like that. My brother of all, his brother would die at the drummer I tell you about. I think he used to play with Sam Offen, the family. He was running around Johnny's age, see. I'm running with Baby. We went to school together, all of us, in Basin, Lewis. And Lorenzo Teo, too, he went to school with us in Basin, Lewis. Really? The whole family had their home over there in Basin, Lewis when I was a kid.
The Teos. Lorenzo Teo. Over in there.
Yes, sir, before we ever come to Georgia. We went to school together.
Was his father over there?
His father and mother was all over there. I don't know what happened to them. Nah.
What about Papai Teo? Was he over there, too?
Papai used to play with my father's family. I thought they were going to tell them that street here.
Next lady, huh?

They lived on Main Street in Basin, Lewis, back Main Street. And we went to school under Professor Brown in Basin, Lewis. Were they Mexican or Spanish or Filipino? No, they were. They looked like they had Indian in them or something. They were. They were. They weren't even Creole. I never heard them talk Creole or nothing like that. They had beautiful black hair. Guys looking big eyes. And they all looked like a nation or something, but they weren't supposed to be.
Did you ever hear young Lorenzo or any of them, his father said they came from Mexico or were ever in Mexico?

I never did know where they came from. All I knew I was a kid in Basin, Lewis, and they were living on Main Street. I used to go to their house. It was the same thing like Baby Dodge would come to my house. My father and their father and mother and all good friends.
Who was Baby Dodge playing with when you took Emma away from you?
Baby was, I think Baby was playing with Celestan. And were you playing with?
No, not with Celestan.
I don't know who he was. You did work with him?
Baby was on the board I believe. Oh yeah. I think he was on the boat. That's what it was. That's right. He was on the boat. Baby did work with Celestan though too.
Oh yeah, he worked with him. Yeah, he worked with him.
Well we could find out when Baby was on the boat and then we could figure out what time.
1918 he went on the boat I think. 1919, 1918 along there.
And that's about the time you joined Celestan though. While Baby was on the boat. Yeah, yeah.
That's right. I mean I didn't know that was my boyfriend.
Well you came back from the war and you say then you worked with the Young Olympia first, didn't you?
Young Olympia band twice. Then the Young Tuxedo band, which Doc Oynos the bass player was the band. Freddie Babu was the trombone player.
Well I want to ask a little bit about that name, Young Tuxedo.
They worked on the Celestan. Everything Celestan couldn't handle he'd give it to us. You understand?
So it wasn't a rival band exactly then. They weren't trying to cash in on the name of the Tuxedo album. Oh no, no.

Celestan used to send us on jobs and things. Called the original Tuxedo and the Young Tuxedo. That's what the name was. I played with them. So it was wild. When I left them I joined Bob Lyons band. When I took Willie Edwards place.
You got his in the Bob Lyons band.
Yeah. Didn't get all the members of the Bob Lyons band. You have the trumpet and who was clarinet? Sidney Bean. That's right. Sidney Bean.

When he was a skeleton trombone. Yes indeed. Yes I worked with him with Bob Lyons band. He worked with us with Bob Lyons band. August Rousseau. He had a mommy shop uptown years ago. Was he a Routiner or what? Was he a Routiner or a reader? He could read. Yeah. Nice old man.
Did he have a play with someone? Yeah. Did he have a play with someone?
Did he have a play with someone? Did he have a play with someone? Did he have a play with someone? Did he have a play with someone?
Did he have a play with someone?
Did he have a play with someone? Nice old man.
Did he ever play with songs then?
He did. He played on the street. He was afraid.
I wanted to ask a little bit more to get back to Bay St. Louis. Over there, Johnny Dobbs. What was he like? Did he play clarinet when he was a boy, when you knew him?
He started on the flute around there while going to school and things like that. That's how you pick up that clarinet.
Was it a little tin flute or a real flute?
No, a little tin flute. That's how Sidney Bissier started.
Did you know Sidney when he was young about the same age as Sidney? What about him? Tell us about Sidney. You must have known him.

I took a girl from Sidney back on Marilyn Johnson when we was in the knee pants. You're an expert at taking girls. When we were in the knee pants, Marilyn Johnson. Our name was B.B. Nice little little Creole guy.
Where did you live about when you moved? Was that before the war or before you went in the army?
That was before the war. Oh, that was before the war.
Where did you live in the city here?
I lived on Marilyn, between Johnston and Gallows.
Where did Sidney be? Sidney lived close around there sometimes.

I lived next door, half a house with Billy Moriah, Simon Moriah, Joe and John Moriah. We were all like a family. Double house. I could hear them over there rehearsing and everything. That's where... Buddy Petit's band was rehearsing in that same house, right next to our house. Simon was playing bass with Buddy. And the father was playing bass with the superior band of them. One of them. Old man Bill Moriah. One of them like I conceived a day. Could Buddy Petit play? Huh? Could Buddy Petit play good? Yeah. He wasn't no high note man, but he played some beautiful down in the stands. Best I've ever heard in my life.
Better than Rene? Huh?

Better than Rene for ragtime? Oh no, no. He wasn't. They were... I mean they both had top notch bands. Uh huh. Rene was a high note man, just like I was. High note. They talk that every day right now in the city. They talk that by Mueller's ball, I'll bum every day right now. Uh huh. That's Rene and Ivy. Now I ain't live trumpet players on the order. Now I'm Perez playing next door to me on Iverville, between Burgundy and Ramport, back in the the Lauderdale Theater. Red Happen was playing with Jordan Overshirt and the Lauderdale. And he was playing at the Black and Tan. I'm playing for Beans, see, at the Eli. Beans, Black Benny, Willie Humphrey, Adolp de Cornshed. Black Benny, Willie, Adolp de Cornshed.
Willie Humphrey, I'll talk to Corsier.

And he could hear me playing over there and he'd tell Willie Humphrey, he'd tell the fellow, come down and say, he's going to bust a vessel in his neck. You see Willie Humphrey, anytime you meet him, just ask him that word. Him and I and Black Benny work together. Years, that he liked.
I've heard a lot of people talk about that. Well, what's more to get back to Johnny Dogg.
Do you remember if he took lessons from anybody? Did he ever? I don't know.
He started out, when he left, way up in the company, he was rotating. I never knew I was doing no reading of it. I took out knowing or saw him reading.
How did he play before he went to Chicago? Was he pretty good or rough or good tone? No, he was clean.

He was good tone. Good tone. Wonderful tone. Variation, beautiful variation and things like that. But I never told him about reading. Well, just like Rene, like I told you, P. Rowe was starting that job on the Rube garden and he had Rene and I to show up to see which one he wanted. He tried both of us on the rehearsal. He wronged and took me. Rene and I showed him and he went on to find his business with his home. He couldn't read fast enough. Louis Armstrong was a very poor reader. Very poor. Couldn't even sign his name. When I was getting the letter from Louis Armstrong and saw the nights he stretched his name down like that. I was surprised. Mills, what I named. His wife there.
Lucille?
No. Oh, Lil. Lil.
Lil. Lil. Lil. Lil Harden. Yeah.

She talked with him just like schooling. You couldn't understand what he was writing when he left here. But now that we're getting mail from him, I got mail from him right there. I keep in my box right now.
You want to save all that? Huh? You want to save all that? That's valuable stuff to have. It's nice. You want me to show you a letter from him? Yeah, we'd like to see it.
I'm going to show you how he edited his letters. We used to get kicks out of it.

Red bean and rice in the yours, Nurse Armstrong. I'm going to show you how to tell the truth. And now that I wrote a letter from him, I see how he scratched his name down there. Like a business man. I said, wow, he went to win at school. He writes nice. I've seen him write. I don't know. I'd like to ask Lawrence Morrero. He knows. Don't forget to get these. I think they're in that between his friends, Johnson and Galbraith. I'm going to show you how to tell the truth. I'm going to show you how to tell the truth. I'm going to show you how to tell the truth.
And now that I'm going to put a letter from him and I see how he scratched his name down there. I'm like a business man. I said, wow, he went to win at school. He writes nice. I've seen him write.
I'm sorry to put the wall back there. Is he still back in that street? I don't know. I'd like to ask Lawrence Morrero. He knows.
Don't forget to get these. I think I have it written down at Tulane. I'm trying to save all that stuff.
See, Ms. Renee is on Condi Street back there, isn't he? I had the old address there.
That's the old address on Condi. She's living on the hardback on that street.
Oh, she doesn't live there.
I've been in the house.
Oh, she's got that address. What is that, Nick? Some thought phone. That's when I was on Clareman Street.
That's one. I cleaned out that box. I don't know where I put it.

It's yellow paper. Yeah, it's green printing. You always use green ink. That's right. You say those would be valuable some days at trading. He writes funny letters. See, we were talking about... I was going to ask if you ever remember that violin player. Maybe that's in your mind now that you were talking about. Was that with the Olympia band or something like that? Another violin player. What was this? Olympia band. I named every violin player I could think of from the...
It's a big odd.
Big odd. Oh, Emil... Big odd. Is it Barney's uncle or somebody? It's his uncle. What can I ask Alan? Yeah, I think that's Emil isn't it?
No, no, no.
Emil he got. Yeah.

That's the man. The bloody man. Yeah, he's the only one that isn't... I took Sidney Devis' place in the Olympia band. Eddie Jackson playing the bass ball. Oh, yeah. I'll never forget that. I've been advertising a mule and wagon. Mule and wagon.
Well, we're talking about bass players. Who did you learn from or did you have lessons in the WPA business or what?
No, I just used to fool with the WPA band. But I went to Kimball. And, uh... Before he bought a house up on 7th Street. He was a kid who was young man. We went up there...
We were talking about Lee Collins. You said he was powerful.
Yes, when Lee came here, he stopped at this hotel on Belmont Street, and he called up his house. My wife and my mother got killed in my car. I was living here alone.
